title: The Shaky Bridge
text:
The Capilano Suspension Bridge in North Vancouver is a narrow walkway of wooden boards and wire cables that sways and tilts some seventy meters above a rocky river. In 1974 the psychologists Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron used it to study attraction.

As men crossed the bridge, an attractive young woman approached them and asked them to fill in a short questionnaire for a class project, which included writing a brief story about an ambiguous picture. When they finished, she tore off a corner of the page, wrote down her name and phone number, and said they could call her if they wanted to hear more about the project. The same procedure was carried out upstream on a solid, low wooden bridge over a small stream.

Men on the frightening bridge wrote stories with more sexual content, and about half of them later called the woman, compared with only a small fraction of the men on the safe bridge. When the interviewer was a man, few men called from either bridge. Dutton and Aron suggested that the men on the swaying bridge had partly misread their pounding hearts and rapid breathing, caused by fear, as attraction to the woman in front of them.
lesson: Strong feelings can come from the situation rather than the person. Before reading too much into a rush of emotion, ask what else might be stirring you up.
location: Capilano Suspension Bridge, North Vancouver, Canada
source: Dutton, D. G., and Aron, A. P. (1974). Some evidence for heightened sexual attraction under conditions of high anxiety. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 30(4), 510-517.
caveat: The samples were small and other explanations are possible, and later studies of arousal and attraction have given mixed results.
